abstract: Low-temperature plasma ejected in solar eruptions can screen active regions as well as quiet solar areas. Absorption phenomena can be observed in microwaves as “negative bursts” and in various spectral domains. We analyze two very different recent events with such phenomena, and present an updated systematic view of solar events associated with negative bursts. Related filament eruptions can be normal, without essential changes of shape and magnetic configuration, and “anomalous.” The latter are characterized by disintegration of an eruptive filament and dispersal of its remnants as a cloud over a large part of the solar disk. Such phenomena can be observed as giant depressions in the He II 304 Å line. One of possible scenarios for an anomalous eruption is proposed in terms of reconnection of the filament's internal magnetic fields with an external large-scale coronal surrounding.

articleTitle: Spatially Resolved Near-Infrared Imaging of a Gravitationally Lensed Quasar, APM 08279+5255, with Adaptive Optics on the Subaru Telescope
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present a spatially resolved imaging analysis of a three-component gravitationally lensed quasar at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ z$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 3.91, APM 08279<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ +$</tex> 5255, in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ L'$</tex>- and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ M'$</tex>-bands, and a narrow band centered at 3.05 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \mu$</tex> m using the 188-element adaptive optics system on the Subaru Telescope. The third, faintest quasar image, component C, has been clearly resolved in all of these bands for the first time. All of the three components are point sources in all three bands. No new component, neither a fourth quasar image nor a lens galaxy, was discovered. The observed bands correspond to the long-wavelength end of the optical power-law continuum of the source quasar in its rest frame, and are little contaminated by strong emission lines like H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha$</tex> . The measured flux ratio of components C to B is shown to be constant in all of the observed bands, and its achromatic nature agrees well with preceding work done at short near-infrared wavelengths one decade ago. On the other hand, the flux ratio of components A to B shows an increase from that of past measurements. This could be ascribed to a microlensing event.

articleTitle: Saturation of StellarWinds from Young Suns
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We investigated mass losses via stellar winds from Sun-like main-sequence stars with a wide range of activity levels. We performed forward-type magnetohydrodynamical numerical experiments for Alfvén wave-driven stellar winds with a wide range of input Poynting flux from the photosphere. Increasing the magnetic field strength and the turbulent velocity at the stellar photosphere from the current solar level, the mass-loss rate rapidly at first increases, owing to suppression of the reflection of the Alfvén waves. The surface materials are lifted up by the magnetic pressure associated with the Alfvén waves, and the cool dense chromosphere is intermittently extended to 10%–20% of the stellar radius. The dense atmospheres enhance the radiative losses, and eventually most of the input Poynting energy from the stellar surface escapes by radiation. As a result, there is no more sufficient energy remaining for the kinetic energy of the wind; the stellar wind saturates in very active stars, as observed in Wood et al. (2002, ApJ, 574, 412; 2005, ApJ, 628, L143). The saturation level is positively correlated with B<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">r,0</inf>f<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0</inf>, where B<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">r,0</inf> and f<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0</inf> are the magnetic field strength and the filling factor of open flux tubes at the photosphere. If B<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">r,0</inf>f<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0</inf> is relatively large ≳5G, the mass-loss rate could be as high as 1000 times. If such a strong mass loss lasts for ∼1 billion years, the stellar mass itself would be affected, which could be a solution to the faint young Sun paradox. We derived a Reimerstype scaling relation that estimates the mass-loss rate from an energetics consideration of our simulations. Finally, we derived the evolution of the mass-loss rates, Ṁ∝t<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1.23</sup>, of our simulations, combining with an observed time evolution of X-ray flux from Sun-like stars, which are shallower than Ṁ∝t<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-2.33±0.55</sup> in Wood et al. (2005).

articleTitle: A New Galactic Extinction Map in High Ecliptic Latitudes
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: In this study, we derived a galactic extinction map in high ecliptic latitudes for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \mid{\beta}\mid$</tex>> 30<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^\circ$</tex> . The dust temperature distribution was derived from the intensities at 100 and 140 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \mu$</tex> m with a spatial resolution of 5<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ '$</tex> . The intensity at 140 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \mu$</tex> m was derived from the intensities at 60 and 100 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \mu$</tex> m of the IRAS data, assuming two tight correlations between the intensities at 60, 100, and 140 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \mu$</tex> m of the COBE/DIRBE data. We found that these correlations can be separated into two correlations by the antenna temperature of the radio continuum at 41 GHz. Because the present study can trace the 5<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ '$</tex>-scale spatial variation in the dust temperature distribution, it has an advantage over the extinction map derived by Schlegel, Finkbeiner, and Davis (1998, ApJ, 500, 525), who used the DIRBE maps to derive the dust temperature distribution with a spatial resolution of 1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^\circ$</tex> . We estimated the accuracy of our method by comparing it with that of Schlegel, Finkbeiner, and Davis (1998, ApJ, 500, 525). The spatial-resolution difference was found to be significant. The area in which the significant difference is confirmed occupies 28% of the region for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \mid{\beta}\mid$</tex>> 30<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^\circ$</tex> . With respect to the estimated extragalactic reddening, the present study has an advantage over the extinction map derived by Dobashi (2011, PASJ, 63, 1), which was based on the 2MASS Point Source Catalog, because our extinction map was derived based on far-infrared emission. Dobashi's extinction map exhibits a maximum value that is lower than that of our map in the galactic plane, and a signal-to-noise ratio that is lower than that of our map in high galactic latitudes. This significant difference is confirmed in 81% of the region for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \mid{\beta}\mid$</tex>> 30<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^\circ$</tex> . In the areas where the significant differences are confirmed, the extinction should be estimated using our method, rather than the previous methods.

articleTitle: A New Cluster of Galaxies Towards the Galactic Bulge, Suzaku J1759–3450
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We observed an extended X-ray source, designated as Suzaku J1759–3450, with Suzaku and Chandra observations towards 1RXS J175911.0–344921, which is an unidentified X-ray source listed in the ROSAT Bright Source Catalogue. A conspicuous emission line at 6 keV was also found in the Suzaku J1759–3450 spectrum. Assuming the emission line to be K emission from He-like Fe ions, we inferred Suzaku J1759–3450 to be an extragalactic object located at z = 0.13. The radial profile of the surface brightness in the 0.5–10 keV band was explained well with an isothermal β-model of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r_\textrm c=1{.^\prime}61$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta=0.78$</tex>. The X-ray spectrum was well reproduced by an opticallythin thermal plasma with the electron temperature of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$kT_e = 5.3$</tex> keV, attenuated by the photoelectric absorption of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N_\textrm H = 2.3 \times 10^{21} \textrm c\textrm m^{-2}$</tex>. The bolometric X-ray luminosity of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_\textrm X(r < r_{500}) = 4.3 \times 10^{44} \textrm {erg} \textrm s^{-1}$</tex> is consistent with that expected from the L<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">X</inf>–T relation of clusters of galaxies. In terms of the spatial extent, the X-ray spectrum, and the bolometric luminosity of the X-ray emitting gas, we concluded that Suzaku J1759–3450 is a new cluster of galaxies.

articleTitle: Suzaku X-Ray Observations of the Accreting NGC 4839 Group of Galaxies and a Radio Relic in the Coma Cluster
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Based on Suzaku X-ray observations, we studied the hot gas around the NGC 4839 group of galaxies and a radio relic in the outskirts of the Coma cluster. We found a gradual decline in the gas temperature from 5 keV around NGC 4839 to 3.6 keV at the radio relic, across which there is a further, steeper drop down to 1.5 keV. This drop as well as the observed surface brightness profile are consistent with a shock with Mach number <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${\cal M} =$</tex> 2.2 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex> 0.5 and velocity <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$v_{\rm s} =$</tex> (1410 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex> 110) km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. A lower limit of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$B > $</tex> 0.33 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex>G was derived based on the magnetic field strength around the relic from the upper limits to inverse Compton X-ray emission. Although this suggests that the non-thermal electrons responsible for the relic are generated by diffusive shock acceleration (DSA), the relation between the measured Mach number and the electron spectrum inferred from radio observations are inconsistent with that expected from the simplest, test-particle theory of DSA. Nevertheless, DSA is still viable if it is initiated by the injection of a pre-existing population of non-thermal electrons. Combined with previous measurements, the temperature profile of Coma in the southwest direction is shallower outside NGC 4839, and also slightly shallower in the outermost region. The metal abundance around NGC 4839 is confirmed to be higher than that in its vicinity, implying a significant peak in the abundance profile that decreases to 0.2 solar toward the outskirts. We interpret these facts as being due to ram pressure stripping of metal-enriched gas from NGC 4839 as it falls into Coma. The relic shock may result from the combined interaction of pre-existing intracluster gas, gas associated with NGC 4839, and cooler gas flowing in from the large-scale structure filament in the southwest.

articleTitle: The Asteroid Catalog Using AKARI IRC Slow-Scan Observations
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present an asteroidal catalog from the mid-infrared wavelength region using the slow-scan observation mode obtained by the Infrared Camera (IRC) on-board the Japanese infrared satellite AKARI. An archive of IRC slow-scan observations comprising about 1000 images was used to search for serendipitous encounters of known asteroids. We have determined the geometric albedos and diameters for 88 main-belt asteroids, including two asteroids in the Hilda region, and compared these, where possible, with previously published values. Approximately one-third of the acquired data reflects new asteroidal information. Some bodies classified as C or D-type with high albedo were also identified in the catalog.

articleTitle: Phase Variation of Earthshine Polarization Spectra
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present the results of the optical spectropolarimetry of Earthshine on the Moon for Earth phase angles ranging from 49<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{\circ}$</tex> to 96<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{\circ}$</tex> . The observations were conducted on 2011 March 9–13 (UT) using the spectropolarimeter HBS installed on the 1.88 m telescope at Okayama Astrophysical Observatory. The wavelength coverage was 450–850 nm with a resolution of 6 nm. The observed Earthshine polarization degree spectra exhibit decreasing polarization degree with increasing wavelength at any phase. The overall degree of polarization increases as the Earth approaches a quadrature phase. The phase dependence differs with the wavelengths; the maximum polarization for the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ V$</tex> band occurs at a phase angle of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim $</tex> 90<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^\circ$</tex>, whereas that for longer wavelengths is reached at larger phase angles. This is interpreted as indicating that Earthshine polarization at shorter wavelengths is dominated by atmospheric Rayleigh scattering, whereas that at longer wavelengths has an increasingly effective contribution from the Earth surface reflection. The wavelength dependence of the phase angle of the maximum polarization appears to be unique among the terrestrial planetary bodies in the Solar System. Therefore, this might constitute important evidence pointing toward a distinctive characteristic of Earth: the planet has a scattering but transparent atmosphere above its surface.

articleTitle: Submillimeter ALMA Observations of the Dense Gas in the Low-Luminosity Type-1 Active Nucleus of NGC1097
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present the first 100 pc scale view of the dense molecular gas in the central ∼1.3 kpc of the type-1 Seyfert NGC 1097, traced by HCN (J = 4–3) and HCO<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">+</sup> (J = 4–3) lines afforded with ALMA band 7. This galaxy shows significant HCN enhancement with respect to HCO<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">+</sup> and CO in the low-J transitions, which seems to be a common characteristic in AGN environments. Using the ALMA data, we consider the characteristics of the dense gas around this AGN, and search for the mechanism of HCN enhancement. We find a high HCN (J = 4–3) to HCO<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">+</sup> (J = 4–3) line ratio in the nucleus. The upper limit of the brightness temperature ratio of HCN (v<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> = 1<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1f</sup>, J = 4–3) to HCN (J = 4–3) is 0.08, which indicates that IR pumping does not significantly affect the pure rotational population in this nucleus. We also find a higher HCN (J = 4–3) to CS (J = 7–6) line ratio in NGC 1097 than in starburst galaxies, which is more than 12.7 on the brightness temperature scale. Combined with similar observations from other galaxies, we tentatively suggest that this ratio appears to be higher in AGN-host galaxies than in pure starburst ones, similar to the widely used HCN to HCO<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">+</sup> ratio. LTE and non-LTE modeling of the observed HCN and HCO<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">+</sup> lines using J = 4–3 and 1–0 data from ALMA, and J = 3–2 data from SMA, reveals a high HCN to HCO<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">+</sup> abundance ratio (5 ≤ [HCN]/[HCO<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">+</sup>] ≤ 20: non-LTE analysis) in the nucleus, and that the high-J lines (J = 4–3 and 3–2) are emitted from dense (10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4.5</sup> cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-3</sup> ≤ n<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">H2</inf> ≤ 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</sup> cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-3</sup>), hot (70K ≤ T<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">kin</inf> ≤ 550 K) regions. Finally we propose that “high-temperature chemistry” is more plausible to explain the observed enhanced HCN emission in NGC 1097 than pure gas-phase PDR/XDR chemistry.

articleTitle: A Fiber Link between the Okayama 188-cm Telescope and the High-Dispersion Spectrograph, HIDES
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have developed a high-efficiency fiber link (HE mode) connecting Okayama 188-cm telescope to the high-resolution spectrograph, HIDES, in order to improve the throughput of the observing system while keeping its radial-velocity measurement precision. In the HE mode, a multi-mode optical fiber collects stellar light within a 2.7-arcsecond diameter field of view (FOV) at the Cassegrain focus, which is twice as large as that of the typical seeing size at our observing site. An image slicer is used at the other end of the link, just in front of the entrance of HIDES, to keep the proper high spectral resolution for such a wide FOV. We have found that the maximum total throughput of the HE mode observations at around 550 nm reaches as high as 9%. Its practical throughput is also found to be more than twice that of the conventional slit observations. We have also confirmed that its reciprocal resolution is over 50000, as designed. The minimum available wavelength, which is determined from an inter-order gap of the echelle spectrum, is about 440 nm, where the gap becomes as narrow as 5 pixels on the CCD detector for the red cross-disperser of HIDES. From measurements of the rms errors of the radial velocity of some stars over one year, the long-term precision is as good as a few m s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex>. The fiber modal noise that could degrade the observed spectra may not be significant in the HE mode, as long as the signal-to-noise ratio of a spectrum is lower than 1500.

articleTitle: Toward Understanding the Anisotropic Point Spread Function of Suprime-Cam and Its Impact on Cosmic Shear Measurement
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We examined the anisotropic point spread function (PSF) of Suprime-Cam data utilizing dense star field data. We decomposed the PSF ellipticities into three components—the optical aberration, atmospheric turbulence, and chip misalignment in an empirical manner—and evaluated the amplitude of each component. We then tested a standard method for correcting the PSF ellipticities used in weak lensing analysis against a mock simulation. We found that, for long-exposure data, the optical aberration has the largest contribution to the PSF ellipticities, which could be modeled well by a simple analytic function based on the lowest-order aberration theory. The statistical properties of PSF ellipticities resulting from atmospheric turbulence were investigated by using numerical simulations. The simulation results are in a reasonable agreement with the observed data. It follows from these findings that the spatial variation of PSF ellipticities consists of two components: one is a smooth and parametrizable component arising from the optical PSF, and the other is a non-smooth and stochastic component resulting from the atmospheric PSF. The former can be well corrected by the standard correction method with a polynomial fitting function. However, for the latter, its correction is affected by the common limitation caused by sparse sampling of PSFs due to a limited number of stars. We also examined the effects of the residual PSF anisotropies on Suprime-Cam cosmic shear data (5.6-degree<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> of i′-band data). We found that the shape and amplitude of the B-mode shear variance are broadly consistent with those of the residual PSF ellipticities measured from the dense star field data. This indicates that most of the sources of residual systematic are understood, which is an important step for cosmic shear statistics to be a practical tool of the precision cosmology.

articleTitle: Multi-Epoch VERA Observations of Sagittarius A*. I. Images and Structural Variability
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on the results of multi-epoch observations of Sgr A<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^*$</tex> with VLBI Exploration of Radio Astrometry (VERA) at 43 GHz, carried out from 2004 to 2008. We detected a time variation of the flux at the 11% level and the intrinsic size at 19%. In addition, comparisons with previous Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) results showed that Sgr A<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^*$</tex> underwent a flaring event for at least longer than 10 d in 2007 May. The intrinsic size of Sgr A<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^*$</tex> remained unchanged within the 1 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sigma$</tex> level from the size before/after the flaring event, indicating that the brightness temperature of Sgr A<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^*$</tex> was increased. The flaring event occurred within 31 d, which is shorter than the refractive time scale. Moreover it is difficult to explain the increase in the spectral index at the flaring event by a simple interstellar scattering model. Hence, the flaring event is most likely associated with changes in the intrinsic properties of Sgr A<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^*$</tex>. We considered the origin of the brightness temperature variation, and concluded that the flaring event of Sgr A<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^*$</tex> could be explained by the continuous heating of electrons, such as a standing shock in accretion flow.

articleTitle: Modeling Line-Driven Disk Wind for Broad Absorption Lines of Quasars
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The disk wind, which is powered by the radiation force due to spectral lines (line force), has been studied concerning broad absorption line (BAL) quasars. We investigated the structure of the disk wind based on a non-hydrodynamic method, and compared it with wind properties inferred from X-ray observations of BAL quasars. In the present work, we applied the stellar wind theory to the initial condition (the mass outflow rate at the base of the wind). We found funnel-shaped winds with a half opening angle of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 50<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{\circ}$</tex> for the case of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \epsilon$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 0.3–0.9 and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ M_{\rm BH}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{7-8.5}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ M_\odot$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \epsilon$</tex> is the Eddington ratio and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ M_{\rm BH}$</tex> is the black-hole mass. Thus, the absorption features are observed for an observer of which the viewing angle is around 50<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{\circ}$</tex> . A probability of BAL quasars is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 7%–11%, which is roughly consistent the abundance ratio of BAL quasars, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 10%–15%. Here, the probability is estimated by the solid angle, that the absorbing features would be detected, divided by 4<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pi$</tex> . In contrast, if the Eddington ratio is smaller than 0.01, or if the black hole is very massive, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ M_{\rm BH}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ >rsim$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{9}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ M_{\odot}$</tex>, the disk wind is not launched due to the less effective line force. Then, the quasars are identified as non-BAL quasars independently of the observer's viewing angle.

articleTitle: An X-Ray Detected Group of Quiescent Early-Type Galaxies at z = 1.6 in the Chandra Deep Field South
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report the discovery of an X-ray group of galaxies located at a high redshift of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ z$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 1.61 in the Chandra Deep Field South. Based on 4 Ms Chandra data, the group is first identified as an extended X-ray source. We have used a wealth of deep multi-wavelength data to identify the optical counterpart—our red sequence finder detects a significant over-density of galaxies at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ z$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 1.6. The brightest group galaxy is spectroscopically confirmed at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ z$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 1.61, based on published spectroscopic redshifts. Using this as a central redshift of the group, we measure an X-ray luminosity of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ L_{0.1{\rm-}2.4\rm keV}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> (1.8 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 0.6) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{43}$</tex> erg s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex>, which then translates into a group mass of (3.2 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 0.8) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{13}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ M_{\odot}$</tex> . This is the lowest-mass group ever confirmed at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ z$</tex>> 1.5. Deep optical–nearIR images from CANDELS reveal that the group exhibits a surprisingly prominent red sequence, and most of the galaxies are consistent with a formation redshift of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ z_{\rm f}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 3. A detailed analysis of the spectral energy distributions of the group member candidates confirms that most of them are indeed passive galaxies. Furthermore, their structural parameters measured from near-IR CANDELS images show that they are morphologically early-type. The newly identified group at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ z$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 1.61 is dominated by quiescent early-type galaxies, and the group appears to be similar to those in the local Universe. One possible difference is the high fraction of AGN—38<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{+23}_{\hskip.4mm-20}$</tex> % of the bright group member candidates are AGN, which might indicate a role for AGN in the quenching of star formation. However, a statistical sample of high-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ z$</tex> groups is needed to draw a general picture of groups at this redshift. Such a sample will hopefully be available in near-future surveys.

articleTitle: Suzaku Detection of Thermal X-Ray Emission Associated with the Western Radio Lobe of Fornax A
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present the results of X-ray mapping observations of the western radio lobe of the FornaxA galaxy, using the X-ray Imaging Spectrometer (XIS) onboard the Suzaku satellite with a total exposure time of 327 ks. The purpose of this study is to investigate the nature and spatial extent of the diffuse thermal emission around the lobe by exploiting the low and stable background of XIS. The diffuse thermal emission had been consistently reported in all previous studies of this region, but its physical nature and relation to the radio lobe had not been examined in detail. Using a data set covering the entire western lobe and the central galaxy NGC1316, as well as comparison sets in the vicinity, we find convincingly the presence of thermal plasma emission with a temperature of ∼1 keV in excess of conceivable background and contaminating emission (cosmic X-ray background, Galactic halo, intra-cluster gas of Fornax, interstellar gas of NGC1316, and the ensemble of point-like sources). Its surface brightness is consistent with having a spherical distribution peaking at the center of the western lobe with a projected radius of ∼12′. If the volume filling factor of the thermal gas is assumed to be unity, its estimated total mass amounts to ∼10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup>M<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">⊙</inf>, which would be ∼10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> times that of the central black hole, and comparable to that of the current gas mass of the host galaxy. Its energy density is comparable to or larger than those in the magnetic field and non-thermal electrons responsible for the observed radio and X-ray emission.

articleTitle: Growth of a Protostar and a Young Circumstellar Disk with a High Mass-Accretion Rate onto the Disk
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The growing process of both a young protostar and a circumstellar disk is investigated. The viscous evolution of a disk around a single star is considered with a model where a disk increases its mass by a dynamically accreting envelope, and simultaneously loses its mass via viscous accretion onto the central star. We focus on a circumstellar disk with a high mass-accretion rate onto the disk, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot{M} =$</tex> 8.512 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$c_{\rm s}^3/G$</tex>, as the result of a dynamical collapse of the rotating molecular cloud core. We consider the origin of the surface density distribution as well as that of the disk-to-star mass ratio by means of numerical calculations of an unsteady viscous accretion disk in a one-dimensional axisymmetric model. It is shown that the radial profiles of the surface density, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Sigma$</tex>, azimuthal velocity, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$v_{\phi}$</tex>, and mass-accretion rate, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot{M}$</tex>, in the inner region approach to the quasi-steady state. The profile of the surface density distribution in a quasi-steady state is determined as to be a result of angular momentum transport, rather than its original distribution of angular momentum in the cloud core. It is also shown that the disk mass becomes larger than the central star in the long-time limit as long as temporally constant mass flux onto the disk is assumed. After the mass infall rate onto the disk declines owing to a depletion of the parent cloud core, the disk-to-star mass ratio, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\rm disk}/M_*$</tex>, decreases. The disk-to-star mass ratio becomes smaller than unity after <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$t > 10^{5}$</tex> yr and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$t > 10^{6}$</tex> yr from the beginning of the accretion phase in the case with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha_{0} =$</tex> 1 and 0.1, respectively, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha_{0}$</tex> is the constant part of the viscous parameter. In the case with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha_{0} \leq 10^{-2}, M_{\rm disk}/M_*$</tex> is still larger than unity at 2 Myr from the beginning of the accretion phase.

articleTitle: X-Ray Observations of the W 51 Complex with Suzaku
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present a detailed analysis of X-ray emission from the middle-aged supernova remnant W 51 C and star-forming region W 51 B with Suzaku. The soft X-ray emission from W 51 C is well-represented by an optically thin thermal plasma in a non-equilibrium ionization state with a temperature of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 0.7 keV. The elemental abundance of Mg is significantly higher than the solar value. We find no significant feature of an over-ionized plasma in W 51 C. The hard X-ray emission is spatially coincident with the molecular clouds associated with W 51 B, overlapping with W 51 C. The spectrum is represented by an optically thin thermal plasma with a temperature of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 5 keV, or a powerlaw model with a photon index of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 2.2. The emission probably has a diffuse nature, since its luminosity of 1 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{34}$</tex> erg s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> in the 0.5–10 keV band cannot be explained by any emission from point sources in this region. We discuss the possibility that the hard X-ray emission comes from stellar winds of OB stars in W 51 B, or accelerated particles in W 51 C.

articleTitle: K-Shell Line Distribution of Heavy Elements along the Galactic Plane Observed with Suzaku
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on the global distribution of the intensities of the K-shell lines from He-like and H-like ions of S, Ar, Ca, and Fe along the Galactic plane. From the profiles, we clearly separate the Galactic center X-ray emission (GCXE) and the Galactic ridge X-ray emission (GRXE). The intensity profiles of the He-like K<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha $</tex> lines of S, Ar, Ca, and Fe along the Galactic plane are approximately similar to each other, while not for the H-like Ly<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha $</tex> lines. In particular, the profiles of H-like Ly<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha $</tex> of S and Fe show remarkable contrast: a large excess of Fe, and almost no excess of S lines in GCXE compared to GRXE. Although the prominent K-shell lines are represented by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 1 keV and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 7 keV temperature plasmas, these two temperatures are not equal between GCXE and GRXE. In fact, a spectral analysis of GCXE and GRXE revealed that the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 1 keV plasma in GCXE has a lower temperature than that in GRXE, and vice versa for the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 7 keV plasma.

articleTitle: Density-Independent Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics for a Non-Ideal Equation of State
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) method is a useful numerical tool to study a variety of astrophysical and planetlogical problems. However, it turned out that the standard SPH algorithm has problems in dealing with hydrodynamical instabilities. This problem is due to the assumption that the local density distribution is differentiable. In order to solve this problem, a new SPH formulation, which does not require the differentiability of the density, was proposed. This new SPH method improved the treatment of hydrodynamical instabilities. This method, however, is applicable only to the equation of state (EOS) of an ideal gas. In this paper, we describe how to extend the new SPH method to non-ideal EOS. We present the results of various standard numerical tests for non-ideal EOS. Our new method works well for non-ideal EOS. We conclude that our new SPH can handle hydrodynamical instabilities for an arbitrary EOS, and that it is an attractive alternative to the standard SPH.

articleTitle: High-Dispersion Spectroscopy of the Superflare Star KIC 6934317
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We conducted high-resolution spectroscopic observation with Subaru/HDS for a G-type star (KIC 6934317). We selected this star from the data of the Kepler spacecraft. It produces many superflares, and the total energy of the largest recorded superflare on this star was ∼10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>-times larger (∼2.2 × 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">35</sup> erg) than that of the most energetic flare on the Sun (∼10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">32</sup> erg). The core depth and the emission flux of the Ca II infrared triplet lines and the Hα line show high chromospheric activity in this star, in spite of its low lithium abundance and small amplitude of the rotational modulation. Using empirical relations between the emission flux of chromospheric lines and the X-ray flux, this star is considered to show much higher coronal activity than that of the Sun. It probably has large starspots that can store a large amount of magnetic energy, sufficient to give rise to superflares. We also estimated the stellar parameters, such as the effective temperature, surface gravity, metallicity, projected rotational velocity (v sin i ), and radial velocity. KIC 6934317 is then confirmed to be an early G-type main-sequence star. The value of v sin i is estimated to be ∼1.91 km s<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup>. In contrast, the rotational velocity is calculated to be ∼20 km s<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup> by using the period of the brightness variation as the rotation period. This difference can be explained by its small inclination angle (nearly pole-on). The small inclination angle is also supported by the contrast between the large superflare amplitude and the small stellar brightness variation amplitude. The lithium abundance and isochrones implies that the age of this star is more than about a few Gyr, though a problem why this star with such an age has such strong activity remains unsolved.

articleTitle: The Possibility of the Kelvin–Helmholtz Instability during Sedimentation of Dust Grains in the Protoplanetary Disk
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We reexamine the possibility of shear-driven turbulence during the sedimentation of dust grains in the protoplanetary disk. Shear-driven turbulence is expected to occur before the onset of a gravitational instability for the MMSN model. However, according to previous studies that did not account of the growth of dust grains, with a larger abundance of dust grains, the gravitational instability is indicated to occur before shear-driven turbulence. In this paper, the case including dust growth is considered, and it is found that a Kelvin–Helmholtz instability tends to occur before the gravitational instability, even in the case with a large abundance of dust grains. This is different from previous results without the dust growth.

articleTitle: Re-Calibration of SDF/SXDS Photometric Catalogs of Suprime-Cam with SDSS Data Release 8
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present photometric recalibrations of the Subaru Deep Field (SDF) and Subaru/XMM-Newton Deep Survey (SXDS). Recently, Yamanoi et al. (2012, AJ, 144, 40) suggested the existence of a discrepancy between the SDF and SXDS catalogs. We have used the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Data Release 8 (DR8) catalog and compared stars in common between SDF/SXDS and SDSS. We confirmed that there exists a 0.12 mag offset in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ B$</tex>-band between the SDF and SXDS catalogs. Moreover, we found that significant zero-point offsets in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ i$</tex>-band (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 0.10 mag) and the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ z$</tex>-band (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 0.14 mag) need to be introduced to the SDF/SXDS catalogs to make it consistent with the SDSS catalog. We report the measured zero point offsets of five filter bands of SDF/SXDS catalogs. We studied the potential cause of these offsets, but the origins are yet to be understood.

articleTitle: An X-Ray Study of the Galactic-Scale Starburst-Driven Outflow in NGC 253
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The X-ray properties of hot interstellar gas in a bright, nearby edge-on starburst galaxy, NGC 253, were investigated so as to gain a further understanding of starburst-driven outflow activity by utilizing XMM-Newton and Suzaku. Spectroscopic analyses for three regions of the galaxy characterized by multiwavelength observations, i.e., the superwind region, the disk region, and the halo region, were conducted. Various emission lines from O, Ne, Mg, Si, and Fe were observed in the spectra of each region. The hot gas was represented by two thin thermal plasmas with temperatures of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ kT$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 0.2 and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 0.6 keV. The abundance ratios, i.e., O<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ /$</tex> Fe, Ne<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ /$</tex> Fe, Mg<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ /$</tex> Fe, and Si<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ /$</tex> Fe, are consistent between the three regions, which suggests a common origin of the hot gas. The abundance patterns are consistent with those of type II supernova ejecta, indicating that the starburst activity in the central region provides metals toward the halo through a galactic-scale starburst-driven outflow. The energetics can also support this indication on the condition that 0.01–50 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \eta^{1/2}$</tex> % of the total emission in the nuclear region has flowed to the halo region. To constrain the dynamics of hot interstellar gas, surface brightness, and hardness ratio profiles, which trace the density and temperature, were extracted. Assuming a simple polytropic equation of state for gas, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ T\rho^{1-\gamma}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> const, we constrained the physical condition; <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \gamma$</tex> is consistent with 5<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ /$</tex> 3 at a hot disk of < 3 kpc from the center along with the minor axis, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ T$</tex> is constant (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \gamma$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 1) in the halo, the distance of which is between 3 and 10 kpc from the center. It is suggested that the hot gas expands adiabatically from the central region towards the halo region while it moves as free expansion from the inner part of the halo towards the outer part of the halo as the outflow. We constrained the outflow velocity to be > 100 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> based on the observed temperature gradient in the halo. In comparison with the escape velocity of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 220 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> for NGC 253, it is indicated that the hot interstellar gas can escape from the gravitational potential of NGC 253 by combining the outflow velocity and the thermal velocity.

articleTitle: Two Power-Law States of the Ultraluminous X-Ray Source IC 342 X-1
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: In order to elucidate the emission properties of ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs) during their power-law (PL) state, we examined long-term X-ray spectral data of IC 342 X-1 during its PL state by using our own Suzaku data and archival data by XMM-Newton, Chandra, and Swift observations. The PL state of this source seems to be classified into two sub-states in terms of the X-ray luminosities in the 0.5–10 keV band: the low-luminosity PL state with (4–6) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{39}$</tex> erg s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> and the high-luminosity one with (1.1–1.4) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{40}$</tex> erg s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> . During Suzaku observations, which were made in 2010 August and 2011 March, X-1 stayed in the low-luminosity PL state. The observed X-ray luminosity (4.9–5.6 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{39}$</tex> erg s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> ) and the spectral shape (photon index <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 1.67–1.83) slightly changed between the two observations. Using the Suzaku PIN detector, we for the first time confirmed a PL tail extending up to at least 20 keV with no signatures of a high-energy turnover in both of the Suzaku observations. In contrast, a turnover at about 6 keV was observed during the high-luminosity PL state in 2004 and 2005 with XMM-Newton. Importantly, the photon indices are similar between the two PL states, and so are the Compton <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ y$</tex>-parameters of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ y$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 1, which indicates a similar energy balance (between the corona and the accretion disk) holding in the two PL states despite different electron temperatures. From spectral similarities with recent studies about other ULXs, and the Galactic black-hole binary GRS 1915<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ +$</tex> 105, IC 342 X-1 is also likely to be in a state with a supercritical accretion rate, although more sensitive higher energy observations would be necessary to make any conclusion.

articleTitle: Can Superflares Occur on Our Sun?
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Recent observations of Sun-like stars, similar to our Sun in their surface temperature (5600–6000 K) and slow rotation (rotational period <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ >$</tex> 10 d), using the Kepler satellite by Maehara et al. (2012, Nature, 485, 478) have revealed the existence of superflares (with energy of 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{33}$</tex> –10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{35}$</tex> erg). From statistical analyses of these superflares, it was found that superflares with energy of 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{34}$</tex> erg occur once in 800 yr, and superflares with 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{35}$</tex> erg occur once in 5000 yr. In this paper, we examine whether superflares with energy of 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{33}$</tex> –10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{35}$</tex> erg could occur on the present Sun through the use of simple order-of-magnitude estimates based on current ideas related to the mechanisms of the solar dynamo. If magnetic flux is generated by differential rotation at the base of the convection zone, as assumed in typical dynamo models, it is possible that the present Sun would generate a large sunspot with a total magnetic flux of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 2 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{23}$</tex> Mx (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> G cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{2}$</tex>) within one solar cycle period, and lead to superflares with an energy of 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{34}$</tex> erg. To store a total magnetic flux of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{24}$</tex> Mx, necessary for generating 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{35}$</tex> erg superflares, it would take <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 40 yr. Hot Jupiters have often been argued to be a necessary ingredient for the generation of superflares, but we found that they do not play any essential role in the generation of magnetic flux in the star itself, if we consider only the magnetic interaction between the star and the hot Jupiter. This seems to be consistent with Maehara et al.'s finding of 148 superflare-generating solar-type stars that do not have a hot Jupiter-like companion. Altogether, our simple calculations, combined with Maehara et al.'s analysis of superflares on Sun-like stars, show that there is a possibility that superflares of 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{34}$</tex> erg would occur once in 800 yr on our present Sun.

articleTitle: Lithium, Carbon, and Oxygen Abundances of Hyades F–G Type Stars
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: In an attempt to carry out a systematic study on the behavior of the photospheric abundances of Li, C, and O (along with Fe) for Hyades main-sequence stars in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ T_{\rm eff}$</tex> range of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 5000–7000 K, we conducted an extensive spectrum-synthesis analysis applied to four spectral regions (comprising lines of Fe-group elements, Li I 6708 line, C I 7111–7119 lines, and O I 6156–8 lines), based on the high-dispersion spectra of 68 selected F–G type stars belonging to this cluster. The abundances of C and O turned out to be fairly uniform in a marginally supersolar level, such as like the case of Fe: <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \langle$</tex> [C<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ /$</tex> H]<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \rangle$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ +$</tex> 0.15 (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sigma$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 0.08), <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \langle$</tex> [O<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ /$</tex> H]<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \rangle$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ +$</tex> 0.22 (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sigma$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 0.14), and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \langle$</tex> [Fe<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ /$</tex> H]<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \rangle$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ +$</tex> 0.11 (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sigma$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 0.08), suggesting that the primordial abundances are almost retained for these elements. Strictly, however, they show a slightly increasing trend with a decrease in <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ T_{\rm eff}$</tex> (typically on the order of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-4}$</tex> dex K<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex>); while this might be due to an improper choice of atmospheric parameters, we found it difficult to give a quantitatively reasonable explanation. Regarding Li, we confirmed the well-known <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ T_{\rm eff}$</tex>-dependent trend in the Li abundance reported so far (a conspicuous Li-trough at 6300 K <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ≲$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ T_{\rm eff}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ≲$</tex> 6700 K and a progressive decrease toward a lower <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ T_{\rm eff}$</tex> at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ T_{\rm eff}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ≲$</tex> 6000 K), which means that the surface Li of Hyades stars is essentially controlled only by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ T_{\rm eff}$</tex>; other parameters, such as the rotational velocity, are almost irrelevant.

articleTitle: Paschen α Observations of Be Stars Toward the SMC Cluster NGC 330
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We made imaging observations of the young SMC cluster NGC 330 in the near-infrared <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ J$</tex>, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ H$</tex>, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ K_{\rm s}$</tex> as well as two narrow-band Pa<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha $</tex> and Pa<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha $</tex>-off filters. The observations were carried out at a high-altitude site, 5640 m, where the atmospheric extinction is small enough to make the spectral range around Pa<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha $</tex> transparent. We present the calibration of specially designed narrow-band filters, and the method used to identify Pa<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha $</tex> emission using photometric colors. We have successfully detected Pa<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha $</tex> emission from almost all Be stars within the detection limit of the small telescope and the narrow-band filters. The strength of Pa<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha $</tex> emission well correlates with that of H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha $</tex>, which also confirms the proper detection of Pa<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha $</tex> emission. This was the first systematic detection of the Pa<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha $</tex> emission line from Be stars. We also found new candidates of Pa<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha $</tex> emission-line objects. This work demonstrates that the photometric colors, including the Pa<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha $</tex> band, can be used to detect the Pa<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha $</tex> line when observed from high-altitude sites.

articleTitle: Multifrequency VLBI Observations of the Broad Absorption Line Quasar J1020 4320: Recently Restarted Jet Activity?
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: This paper reports on very-long-baseline interferometry observations of the radio-loud broad absorption line (BAL) quasar J1020<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ +$</tex> 4320 at 1.7, 2.3, 6.7, and 8.4 GHz using the Japanese VLBI network (JVN) and European VLBI network (EVN). The radio morphology is compact with a size of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 10 pc. The convex radio spectrum has been stable over the last decade; an observed peak frequency of 3.2 GHz is equivalent to 9.5 GHz in the rest frame, suggesting an age on the order of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 100 years as a radio source, according to an observed correlation between the linear size and the peak frequency of compact steep spectrum (CSS) and giga-hertz peaked spectrum (GPS) radio sources. A low-frequency radio excess suggests a relic of past jet activity. J1020<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ +$</tex> 4320 may be one of the quasars with recurrent and short-lived jet activity during a BAL-outflowing phase.

articleTitle: An X-Ray Counterpart of HESS J1427−608 Discovered with Suzaku
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on the discovery of an X-ray counterpart of the unidentified very high-energy gamma-ray source HESS J1427<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 608. In the sky field coincident with HESS J1427<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 608, an extended source was found in the 2–8 keV band, and was designated as Suzaku J1427–6051. Its X-ray radial profile has an extension of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sigma$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 0<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ .\!\!'$</tex> 9 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 0<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ .\!\!'$</tex> 1 if approximated by a Gaussian. The spectrum was well fitted by an absorbed power-law with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ N_{\rm H}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> (1.1 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 0.3) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{23}$</tex> cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-2}$</tex>, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Gamma$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 3.1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{+0.6}_{-0.5}$</tex>, and the unabsorbed flux <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ F_{\rm X}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> (9<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{+4}_{-2}$</tex>) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-13}$</tex> erg s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-2}$</tex> in the 2–10 keV band. Using XMM-Newton archive data, we found seven point sources in the Suzaku source region. However, because their total flux and absorbing column densities are more than an order of magnitude lower than those of Suzaku J1427–6051, we consider that they are unrelated to the Suzaku source. Thus, Suzaku J1427–6051 is considered to be a truly diffuse source and an X-ray counterpart of HESS J1427<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 608. The possible nature of HESS J1427<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 608 is discussed based on the observational properties.

articleTitle: Observations and Orbital Analysis of the High-Amplitude Delta Scuti Star SZ Lyncis: The Unusual Orbital Precession
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We determined forty-two new times of light maximum from our photometry observations and WASP project, and collected all times of light maximum observed between 1961 and 2013 in order to calculate the orbital elements of the SZ Lyncis system and the secular change of the pulsation period with the classical <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$O-C$</tex> method. We confirmed the decrease of the longitude of the periastron passage with a rate of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(-1.^{\circ}15 \pm 0. ^{\circ}25 )\textrm {yr}^{-1}$</tex>, and discussed the causative mechanism. The results show that the precession of the star's orbit might be due to a close binary system, which means that the companion of SZ Lyncis is actually a binary system. We used the Hipparcos Intermediate Astrometric Data to obtain the complete orbital elements of the SZ Lyncis system, and found that the inclination, i, and parallax, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pi_{t}$</tex>, are <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$39.^{\circ}5 \pm 17.^{\circ}7$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2.^{\circ}61\pm 0.^{\circ}98$</tex> mas (corresponds to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$380 \pm 140$</tex>), respectively. We reanalyzed the mean radial velocities of SZ Lyncis given by Bardin and Imbert (1984), and noticed a weak variation existing in the residuals from a single-Keplerian fit. We suggest that more detailed high-precision spectroscopic observations are definitely needed in the future to check this short periodic change.

articleTitle: Kinetic Scheme for Solving the M1 Model of Radiative Transfer
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We show a numerical scheme to solve the moment equations of radiative transfer, i.e., the M1 model, which follows the evolution of the energy density, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$E$</tex>, and the energy flux, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\boldsymbol{F}$</tex>. In our scheme we reconstruct the intensity from <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$E$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\boldsymbol{F}$</tex>, so that it is consistent with the closure relation, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\chi = \left(3+4f^2\right)/ \big({\rm 5}+{\rm 2}\sqrt{4-3 f^2}\big)$</tex>. Here, the symbols <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\chi, f = \vert\boldsymbol{F}\vert/$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$cE$</tex>), and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$c$</tex>, denote the Eddington factor, the reduced flux, and the speed of light, respectively. We evaluate the numerical flux across the cell surface from the kinetically reconstructed intensity. It is an explicit function of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$E$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\boldsymbol{F}$</tex> in the neighboring cells across the surface considered. We include absorption and reemission within a numerical cell in evaluating the numerical flux. The numerical flux approaches the diffusion approximation when the numerical cell, itself, is optically thick. Our numerical flux gives a stable solution even when some regions computed are very optically thick. We show the advantages of the numerical flux with examples. They include a flash of beamed photons and irradiated protoplanetary disks.

articleTitle: Analysis of a Kepler Light Curve of the Novalike Cataclysmic Variable KIC 8751494
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We analyzed a Kepler light curve of KIC 8751494, a recently recognized novalike cataclysmic variable in the Kepler field. We detected a stable periodicity of 0.114379(1) d, which we identified as being the binary’s orbital period. The stronger photometric period at around 0.12245 d, which had been detected from a ground-based observation, was found to be variable, and we identified this period as the positive-superhump period. This superhump period showed short-term (10–20 d) strong variations in period most unexpectedly when the object entered a slightly faint state. The fractional superhump excess varied by as much large as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 30%. The variation of the period very well traced the variation of the brightness of the system. The time-scale of this variation of superhump periods was too slow to be interpreted as a variation caused by a change of the disk radius due to thermal disk instability. We interpreted the cause of the period variation as a varying pressure effect on the period of positive superhumps. This finding suggests that the pressure effect, in at least novalike systems, plays a very important (up to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 30% in the precession rate) role in producing the period of positive superhumps.
